Name: Leah
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. Can you tell me how you came to be working from home, and what it's like for you now?

Name: Toby
Transcript: Yeah, so, I'm a, my title is digital marketing executive, which sounds grander than it is. I do social media for a group of garden centres, mostly. And I started in September 2021, so I've never really known anything else. I did my interview on Zoom, I got my laptop in the post, and my first day was me in my bedroom with a box. And the agency's got an office in Manchester, technically, but it's hot-desking and Tuesdays and Thursdays are meant to be office days, but half the team don't come in, so you go in and you sit with headphones on next to someone you've never spoken to, and then you go home. So mostly I don't bother. What's it like? Honestly? It's a bit grim. I don't want to sound ungrateful. But I'm twenty-seven and I spend most of my life in one room.

Name: Leah
Transcript: One room.

Name: Toby
Transcript: I live in a house share. Four of us. My room's got the bed, the wardrobe, and a desk I got off Facebook Marketplace that's slightly too small. And that's it. That's my office and my bedroom and my living room, because the actual living room's a bit, it's where Callum plays FIFA.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you take me through a normal working day, from when you get up?

Name: Toby
Transcript: So the bad version or the good version? The bad version is I wake up at eight fifty-five, and I roll over and I open the laptop on the bed and I'm online by nine. With my camera off, obviously. And then I'm sort of half in bed doing scheduling till about eleven, and I feel disgusting. The good version is I set an alarm for half seven, I go out and get a coffee from the place at the end of the road, walk round the block, and come back and sit at the desk like a person. I'd say it's about fifty fifty. Maybe sixty forty bad. Then it's, you know, posts, reporting, Slack, Slack, Slack. Lunch I'll make something in the kitchen and bring it back up. And I sort of stop around half five. Ish.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You said Slack three times.

Name: Toby
Transcript: Yeah. Because it's constant. And I'm very aware of the little green dot. That's a big thing for me. If my dot goes yellow, because I've been away from the laptop for ten minutes, I feel like someone's going to notice. Which they're not, I know they're not. My manager's lovely. But I'll get up to go to the toilet and I'll wiggle the mouse before I go. I've actually thought about getting one of those things that moves your mouse for you. A mouse jiggler. I haven't. But I've looked at them.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What is it you think someone would notice?

Name: Toby
Transcript: That I'm not working. That I'm, like, skiving. Because nobody can see me. In an office, people can see you're there. You're at your desk, you look busy, job done. At home, all they've got is the dot and how fast you answer. So I answer really fast. Like, within a minute. Which means I'm never actually concentrating on anything, because I'm always waiting for the ping.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Where in your home do you work? What's that space like for you?

Name: Toby
Transcript: The bedroom. At the little desk. And the thing is, it means I sleep at work. That's how it feels. I'm lying in bed at night and the laptop's right there, about a metre from my head, and sometimes the light on the side of it is flashing because it's charging and I can see it on the ceiling. I started putting a t-shirt over it. Like a birdcage. Which my girlfriend thinks is hilarious.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What does the t-shirt do for you?

Name: Toby
Transcript: It just means it's gone. For the night. I can't put it anywhere else because there isn't anywhere else. So I cover it up. It's stupid but it works, a bit.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What happens at the start and the end of your working day?

Name: Toby
Transcript: Depends on the day, really. On a good day, the walk to the coffee place is me starting. I sort of go out as one person and come back as a worker. And the end is when I put the t-shirt on the laptop, I suppose. But on a bad day it doesn't start, it just sort of seeps in. And it doesn't finish either. I'll be watching something on my phone at ten and I'll see a notification from a client and I'll just reply. From bed. Because it's easier than lying there knowing it's sitting there.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You said you go out as one person and come back as a worker. What's the difference?

Name: Toby
Transcript: The worker's got his shoes on, for a start. No, it's, I think the worker's sort of sharper. He's got a plan for the day. The other one's just a lad in a bedroom who's a bit behind on everything. And the walk is the only thing that turns one into the other. If I don't do it, I'm the lad in the bedroom all day, just with a laptop.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How has working from home changed things with the people you live with, or the people around you?

Name: Toby
Transcript: The housemates are all out at work, apart from Priya, who's a nurse, so she's on nights a lot and she's asleep in the day. So I have to be really quiet on calls, which is a whole thing. I take calls whispering sometimes. My manager once asked if I was in a library. With my parents, my mum keeps saying, it must be lovely, you can do your washing in the day. And I'm like, Mum, I'm working. And she's like, yeah, but you're at home. I don't think she really believes it's a job. And I get that, because some days I'm not sure I do either.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You're not sure it's a job.

Name: Toby
Transcript: Not that it's not a job. That I'm, I don't know if I'm good at it. Because nobody's ever sat next to me. You know when you start somewhere and you learn by listening to people? How they talk on the phone, how they handle a difficult client, what they find funny. I never got any of that. I learnt everything off a screen share. So I don't really know what a good marketing person sounds like. I've only ever heard them on Teams.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you tell me about a day working from home that has stayed with you?

Name: Toby
Transcript: Yeah, so, Priya, the nurse. There was one week where she was on nights and I had this massive pitch, like a big presentation to a new client, the biggest thing I'd done. And she was asleep next door, and the walls are paper. And I ended up doing the whole thing from my car. In the street. With the laptop on the steering wheel and the hotspot on my phone. And it went fine, actually, they signed. But I remember thinking, this is my big moment and I'm in a Fiesta outside a chicken shop.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What was that like, in the car?

Name: Toby
Transcript: Funny, now. At the time I was a bit, I just felt like I didn't have a proper place to be a professional. Like I was pretending. Playing at work.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What, if anything, do you miss about working somewhere else? And what would you miss if you had to go back?

Name: Toby
Transcript: It's weird to miss something you never had. But I miss, I think I miss the in-between bits. Like, making a tea and someone's there and you have a moan about the client. Going to the pub on a Friday. Actually having colleagues, not just, like, names. I know what my manager's kitchen looks like. I've never seen her legs. That's a strange thing to know about someone. What would I miss if I had to go back? Probably the lie-ins, if I'm honest. And not having to pay for the train. That's about it. I'd go back tomorrow if everyone else did.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Is there anything about working from home that we haven't touched on, that matters to you?

Name: Toby
Transcript: Just that everyone talks about it like it's a perk. And for some people it is. My dad would love it. But I think for people my age, starting out, it's a bit like being told you've won something you didn't enter. And then not being allowed to say you don't want it.
